classification.difficultyReason: Requires counterexamples involving a double root and a disconnected function domain.

children.label: a
children.prompt: If $P(x)$ is a cubic with a double root at $x=a$, then the solution to $P(x)\ge 0$ is a single interval $[a,\infty)$ for some value of $a$.

answer.worked:
Consider $P(x)=x^3-x^2=x^2(x-1)$, which has a double root at $x=0$. Its graph touches the $x$-axis at $0$ and crosses it at $1$. It is negative elsewhere to the left of $1$ and positive to the right of $1$.

Thus $P(x)\ge 0$ has solution $\{0\}\cup[1,\infty)$, which is not a single interval.

spec.description: Authored counterexample graph with the isolated equality point at zero and crossing at one.
spec.mathematics: P(x)=x^2(x-1); P(x)>=0 exactly at x=0 and for x>=1.

children.label: b
children.prompt: If $y=f(x)$ and $y=g(x)$ do not have any points of intersection, then the graph of $f$ is either purely above $g$ or purely below $g$.

answer.worked: Consider $f(x)=\dfrac{1}{x}$ and $g(x)=0$. Their graphs do not intersect. However, $f$ is above $g$ when $x>0$ and below $g$ when $x<0$. The value $x=0$ is outside the domain of $f$.

spec.description: Authored counterexample showing different above/below relationships on the two components of the reciprocal function's domain.
spec.mathematics: 1/x is positive for x>0, negative for x<0, undefined at zero, and never zero.
